title.rendered: Jehovah Raah, the Lord Is My Shepherd: The Gospel For Today

excerpt.rendered: David, who had once been the shepherd, wrote of the greater Shepherd: Jehovah Raah, the Lord who leads, feeds, and stays close in the valley.

content.rendered:
David, who had once been the shepherd, wrote of the greater Shepherd: Jehovah Raah, the Lord who leads, feeds, and stays close in the valley.

The Gospel For Today | Sunday, August 16, 2026

Today’s Scripture

“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
Psalm 23:1 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

No one wrote about shepherding like a man who had actually done it. Before David was king, he was the boy left with the sheep while his brothers were considered for anointing, the one who fought a lion and a bear to protect a flock nobody else was watching (1 Samuel 16:11, 17:34-36). When David called God his shepherd, he was not reaching for a pretty metaphor. He was describing, from firsthand experience, exactly what a good shepherd does — and telling us God does all of it for him.

Jehovah Raah is not in the text as a formal title the way Jehovah Jireh or Jehovah Rapha are, but the entire twenty-third psalm is built to unpack what it means. A shepherd makes the sheep lie down in green pastures, because sheep will not rest if they are anxious. A shepherd leads beside still waters, because sheep will not drink from anything turbulent. A shepherd restores the soul, walks through the valley of the shadow of death without flinching, and prepares a table even with enemies watching.

The English Standard Version keeps the whole psalm’s economy intact: “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.” (Psalm 23:1 ESV). Six words carrying an entire theology of provision, guidance, protection, and presence. Not “I shall not want for anything specific,” but simply, “I shall not want” — the lack itself is removed as a category, because the Shepherd is sufficient.

Jesus later claimed this identity outright: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). David’s shepherd led sheep to pasture; Christ, the greater Shepherd, laid down His own life so the sheep could live. Every comfort David described in Psalm 23 — the rest, the guidance, the table in the presence of enemies, the goodness and mercy following all the days of his life — is available now on resurrection ground, secured by a Shepherd who did not just walk through the valley of the shadow of death alongside us, but walked through death itself and came out the other side.

If you feel unshepherded today — anxious, thirsty, wandering, or watched by enemies — Jehovah Raah has not stepped away from the flock. He is still leading, still restoring, still setting the table.

Prayer

Father, You are Jehovah Raah, my Shepherd. I lay down my anxiety and let You lead me to rest. I lay down my striving and let You lead me to still waters. Restore what feels worn down in my soul today. Walk with me through whatever valley I am in, and let me trust Your rod and staff instead of my own fear. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

My God is Jehovah Raah, my Shepherd. I shall not want. He leads me, feeds me, and restores my soul. Even in the valley, I will fear no evil, for He is with me.
